confidence_note: Book text not read; Kodak/Instagram from PopMatters and search summaries; bounty/spread from Wikipedia. Digital-goods claim (copied at near-zero cost, perfectly, instantly) rests on general knowledge of the book. Omitted: WhatsApp 55 employees (post-dates the book), 1990 cassette vs 2005 torrent, GDP-as-welfare claims beyond 'inadequate'.
facts: Kodak employed over 145,000 people directly, a third in Rochester, New York, plus thousands via dealers and distributors; Instagram, built on digital photo data, had 15 employees.
The authors use the pair to argue the digital economy can create value without creating many jobs.
Digital goods can be copied at close to zero cost, perfectly and instantly.
Bounty: the growing number, diversity and quality of goods at falling prices; GDP is inadequate to measure it.
Spread: growing differences in wealth, income and mobility; drivers: skill-biased technical change, capital income rising relative to labour income, superstar effects.
The authors argue for maximising bounty and limiting spread; the Washington Post called the policy proposals reasonable but straight from tech executives' long-peddled talking points.
scene_details: Kodak's headquarters in Rochester, New York
tension: One company needed 145,000 people for photography, another 15.

lessons.idea: Ask what one more customer costs before judging a plan.
lessons.anchor: digital goods copied at near-zero cost

reflect_final: In your work, what does one more customer, reader or user cost you in time right now?

use_cases.situation: Planning a product and team size
use_cases.move: Ask what one more customer costs in people.

use_cases.situation: Choosing a skill or side project
use_cases.move: Contrast 145,000 with 15 and ask which skill still pays when copied.

use_cases.situation: Friend says free apps cost nothing
use_cases.move: Ask what free app they would pay for if it vanished.

pocket_idea: When copies cost almost nothing, a small team can reach a huge audience; ask what one more customer costs.
